prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy, with the first controlled study of interactions in a clock of many atoms

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. The discovery is one idea and its consequences. Katori showed that there is a wavelength at which the optical trap shifts the two clock levels equally, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held at once without the trap spoiling the transition. Ye's group turned this into the record-accuracy clock and, importantly for me as a theorist, into a laboratory for many-body physics: they studied collisional and interaction shifts, spin-orbit and lattice effects, and coherence in a clock of many atoms. Independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg now agree at the 1e-18 level and compare clocks across sites, which is the reproduction I ask for. The measurable consequences are not only metrological: gravitational redshift is resolved over millimetres to centimetres, and the clocks put limits on drifting constants and on new couplings. I would word the citation so that it rests on what has been demonstrated, not on the future redefinition of the second. The 2005 comb prize made optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems, but neither contains the magic-wavelength lattice idea. After the first round I find the case on maturity and attribution stronger than it was, because nobody has proposed a credit other than Katori and Ye, and I have thought about the early priority claims and still believe the two names are right.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is novelty: a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the best result in a line of precision-measurement work already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and as an instrument whose largest payoff, the redefinition of the second, is still ahead. A second objection is credit. Takamoto and Katori published the first lattice clock in 2005, the SYRTE group of Lemonde reached comparable early results, and the NIST groups of Ludlow and Hinkley set later accuracy milestones, so any two-name prize passes over people who did real work. Third, Ye's role is partly a matter of systematics control and engineering, and a committee that wants nature to do something unexpected may prefer moire matter (B003) or lattice quantum simulation (B014). I also remain close to this field as a theoretical atomic physicist, and I know it is easy for me to overrate a result whose physics I understand well.

responses.point: Pearce asks me, as an atomic physicist, to judge whether Lemonde or Ludlow have a claim that a two-name prize would unfairly pass over, and says the citation should rest on what is demonstrated, not a promised redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on the citation, and I have tried to write mine so that it names only demonstrated results: the invention, the 1e-18 accuracy, and the study of interactions among many atoms. On Lemonde, my view is that the SYRTE group made an important early and independent demonstration and later contributed to the comparison of clocks, but the proposal and the first realisation, with the key insight about the magic wavelength, belong to Katori. On Ludlow and Hinkley, their results are milestones in accuracy and systematics, and Ye's group, which also reached 1e-18, is the one whose work covers both the record numbers and the physics of the many-atom clock. If someone shows me a primary paper in which the magic-wavelength concept was independently arrived at, I would reconsider. I do not know of one, and I would want the committee's expert reports checked on that point. I also disclose that my judgement here is that of a theorist who reads these papers, not of someone who builds the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll shares my view that the redefinition of the second should not be a condition, and wants the many-body and interaction physics inside the clock considered for the citation.
responses.response: Thank you for pushing on the many-body point; I have now put it into the citation, as a short clause on interactions in a clock of many atoms, because it is what makes the lattice clock a physics result and not only a measurement. I would keep it modest. The clause should not imply that Ye alone did the many-body work, and I would not want to claim more for the interaction physics than the experiments have shown. I also agree with your resistance to widening the credit to name SYRTE and NIST. A third name would raise the question of why not the fourth and the fifth, and the committee's three-person limit would then force a choice that the history does not support. I note your lineage link to Hall and Ye. As I said, I have no such link to Katori or Ye myself, but my guess is that this does not change the scientific assessment, and I would not ask you to recuse yourself on this basis.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, argues that the open mechanism is the sign of a living field, and says he would be content to see B024 taken first if B003 needs more time.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I agree that an open mechanism is not a bar in itself. The Nobel Prize has honoured discoveries whose explanation came later. My caution about B003 is specific: the flat-band prediction is clean, but the experimental credit is spread over Cao, Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others, and a three-name credit with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero compresses a very broad experimental effort into one laboratory. That tension may ease as the field consolidates, and the twist-angle disorder problem may become better understood. I would therefore be happy to see B003 recognised in a later year. If you are asking whether I could accept B003 in 2026, the honest answer is that I could, with Bistritzer, but it would not be my choice, and I would rather give the clock this year because it has no comparable attribution problem.

responses.point: Johansson wants the citation to name the lattice scheme specifically, not clocks in general, and distinguishes the neutral-atom magic-wavelength interrogation from the ion-clock and comb recognitions.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed the citation wording to follow your suggestion: it now names the optical lattice clock and its invention rather than a general advance in atomic clocks. I would defend the distinction you make. The ion clock gains in accuracy by controlling a single particle; the lattice clock gains by using a very large number of neutral atoms in a trap that does not perturb the transition, and that is why the statistical precision and the study of many-body effects are so different. The comb is the ruler that reads the oscillation and is not the clock. Where I would add a caution is the word 'discovery'. I think the right claim is an invention with a demonstrated outcome, and I would not want us to claim more novelty than that, since several colleagues are sensitive to this point.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active matter (B006) first and the chair's summary records that I and Johansson asked which experiments quantitatively test the Toner-Tu exponents; he also says he would not seriously oppose colleagues on B024.
responses.response: I am grateful for that, and for the candour about the partial experimental tests. As an atomic physicist I cannot judge the quality of the exponent measurements in colloidal and bacterial systems myself, so I read your own reservation as a real one, not a rhetorical one: if the tests of the exponents are partial, then the strongest part of the case, the universality of the hydrodynamic theory, has not yet been checked as thoroughly as the prediction deserves. The omission of Tu also troubles me, because the continuum theory is joint work with Toner. I see the minimal-model argument and I find it elegant, but I cannot put it ahead of a result that has been reproduced in several laboratories at a stated precision. If other members can point to quantitative tests, I would be glad to hear them before the vote.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the historical record of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations be checked and finds B014's attribution harder than the clocks, with four names for a three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree on both points. On the record: the proposal of the magic wavelength is Katori's, and the first demonstration of a lattice clock with Sr is the 2005 Takamoto and Katori paper, with the 2006 papers from Ye's and Lemonde's groups following soon after. The primary papers are open to the committee's experts, and I believe the dates support a clear Katori priority for the concept. On B014, I accept your point and I keep it as an alternative, not as a lead, for the reason you give: the split between theory (Jaksch, Zoller) and experiment (Greiner, Bloch, Esslinger) cannot be resolved with three names without leaving out someone whom a reader of the history would expect to see, and I would not want to force that choice in order to avoid a different one.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the discovery claim and the mechanism claim in twisted bilayer graphene are separable and that the Nobel Prize has preceded a settled mechanism before, and says he would not oppose B024 as a strong second choice.
responses.response: I accept that distinction. The correlated insulators and the superconducting domes are reproduced, and I do not require a final theory of pairing before I would call it a discovery. What keeps me from putting B003 first is the combination of three things at once: the mechanism, the twist-angle disorder that makes samples differ, and a three-name credit that cannot cover the experiments. Any one of these I would tolerate. Together they say that the field will be easier to recognise fairly in a few years. I am glad that you regard B024 as a strong second choice, and I think this means that, whatever the committee decides, B024 is a configuration few of us would be unhappy with, and that matters for a prize that has to be defended in public.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a distinct invention and not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 recognitions; I believe it is, but this is a judgement and not a measurement.

Whether the priority of Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley for particular demonstrations requires a change in credit; I have checked this from memory and from the published record, not against the primary papers, and I would welcome a check by the committee's experts.
How much weight to give to the pending redefinition of the second; I would give it none in the citation, but others may weigh timing differently.
Whether B003 will be judged mature enough in another year or two, which would affect whether I prefer to wait with the clock or with the moire platform if the committee is split.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye and I have not co-authored with the lattice-clock groups. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, which does not involve any shortlisted name. I work in theoretical atomic physics, adjacent to B024 and B014, and I have flagged this closeness of field as a possible bias, not as a ground for recusal. Having heard colleagues, I still do not think recusal is warranted. I also note Kroll's lineage connection through Hall and Ye and do not regard it as a reason for him to withdraw.
